title: Report on Studying Abroad at Adelaide University
paragraphs: I was allowed to study at the University of Adelaide in Australia. Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, a safe, small and lovely city that is easy to live in. The wine and cheese are delicious, and apparently it has the largest number of restaurants per person in Australia (whether the number of restaurants itself is large, or it is a matter of the number of residents, I do not know). It is also a city of music, and in the mall in the city centre the songs of street musicians of all genres, from upbeat rap to traditional Chinese music, never cease. Here, for three months, I lived in a small apartment shared with two girls from Nagoya University.

The departments in which I was looked after in my clerkship were, in order, emergency, hematology and pediatrics. The first two departments were at the Royal Adelaide Hospital, and the last, pediatrics, was at the Women's and Children's Hospital.

First, the department that looked after me in the first month was the Emergency Department. It is divided into area A, area B, resuscitation and short stay, and one moves freely between the four areas. In areas A and B, the flow was to interview and examine walk-in patients, present to the doctor including the differential and plan, and do physical examinations and procedures together with the doctor. Because I was doing interviews in English of a kind I had hardly ever done even in Japan, at first I was bewildered by everything, but at such times the local students helped me a great deal. True to Australia, a country of immigrants, many of the doctors and students had various backgrounds, from the UK, Korea, Malaysia, India and Vietnam, and it was very stimulating.

The next department I visited was haematology. Here I moved back and forth between the lab, the ward and the outpatient clinic. What was impressive was the small-group PBL for students. With one doctor and four students including me, we discussed a given case of a blood disease. How to interpret the symptoms and test results, what to think and what to do next. Even though it is also PBL, the atmosphere was quite different from what I had experienced in my fourth year. The students said what they thought outright, and I did not sense any hesitation such as "what if I am wrong." It was an atmosphere of whoever speaks up wins. When I was in Emergency, I was often amazed at the local students' high communication skills, but seeing the educational setting in Haematology, I was convinced that they become like that because they have received this kind of education for many years. In Japan, I think there were fewer opportunities to practise stating one's own way of thinking. Also, I felt that education here goes further into practical matters than in Japan. In fact, I was told that students have countless OSCE exams before graduating. Being able to see an educational setting different from Japan's in the position of a student, I think I gained the eye to see the good points and points for improvement of both objectively, which was a very valuable experience.

Also, for a short time, I asked and was allowed to visit the burns unit as well. It is a large facility that accepts patients from a vast area into which Japan could fit about four or five times. It was the first time I saw skin graft surgery and it was very interesting. What was very impressive was how they responded to a patient who burst into tears out of fear during a hand skin graft operation under local anesthesia. The doctor who cracked jokes to make them laugh, the student (a student, mind you!) who took off the mask and encouraged the patient with firm eye contact, and the operating room nurse who put on cheerful music and started dancing were all, I thought, true specialists who care even for the patient's psychological side.

Last, I visited pediatrics. Within pediatrics, the sections are clearly divided here, and of several I visited the general, respiratory, and allergy/immunology sections. I followed the doctors on rounds and in the clinic, asking this and that and doing physical examinations. When I had got used to it, I was sometimes entrusted with things like "Could you check whether that child has meningeal signs?", and at such times I felt both the joy of being trusted with it and a tightening of resolve that it would be serious if I made a mistake.

Before the study abroad I was full of anxiety rather than expectation, but once it started, I was absorbed every day and before I knew it the day of my return home had come. From the preparation stage of the study abroad until after my return home, I received great support from truly many people. I am sincerely grateful to have been given such a valuable opportunity. Thank you very, very much.
